prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B005 alone, Katori and Ye. After reading all eight first-round statements, the answer to the chair's first question is, I think, short enough to put in one sentence. The 2005 prize gave the means to count optical cycles and the 2012 prize gave control of a single trapped ion; the lattice clock is the invention that holds thousands of neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, so that motional and light-shift errors cancel while the many-atom signal is read out. That is a different physical mechanism, not the same device made better, and it is what took the stability and accuracy to the 1e-18 level in more than one laboratory. For my criterion of the original experiment, verified, this is the clearest case on the list: the proposal and first realization are traceable to Katori, the record accuracy and many-body control to Ye, and RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, SYRTE and NIST have since reproduced and compared the clocks. It is also a tool that opens a door, with relativistic geodesy, constant-variation tests and dark-matter searches already under way. Eight of eight members stating the same two names is unusual and I treat it as a sign that the credit question is better settled here than for any alternative, not as a substitute for the primary-source checks.
statement.case_against: The overlap with 2005 and 2012 has not disappeared, and I do not want to dismiss it. If the citation is drafted loosely, the prize will read as a third reward for the comb and for precision metrology. It is also still a measurement achievement, so a colleague who holds that a Nobel discovery must reveal a new phenomenon can reasonably vote differently; I would answer that the statutes say discovery or invention, but I accept that this is a judgment and not a proof. The credit outside the two names (Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Derevianko) is real and a two-person configuration cannot represent it. Finally, the primary-source chronology, in particular Katori's 2001-2003 proposal against the first strontium lattice-clock measurements, is something I have not been able to verify from the files and would want confirmed by outside experts before a final decision.

responses.point: Eriksson asks whether the many-atom lattice step is a real conceptual advance over single-ion clocks or mainly a gain in averaging, and says he relies on colleagues from atomic physics because it is outside his expertise.
responses.response: As an experimentalist I would say it is more than averaging. A single ion gives superb accuracy but a poor signal-to-noise ratio, so averaging takes very long; a lattice with thousands of atoms improves stability, but only because the magic wavelength cancels the light shift and the tight confinement removes Doppler and recoil effects. Without that trapping idea, many neutral atoms would simply give a larger systematic error. So the many-atom step and the trapping step are one invention, and that is what I would put in the answer to the chair. I would still ask Lindroth and Kroll to confirm the atomic-physics wording, since they know the field better than I do.

responses.point: Johansson lists the pending SI redefinition, the overlap with 2005 and 2012, and the possibility of a third name for the lattice-clock lineage as open points.
responses.response: My position on timing is the same as in round 1: I would not wait for the redefinition. It is a decision by metrology bodies, and what we have to judge is the verified physics, which already exists in the comparisons at 1e-18. If the redefinition came first it would help the case, but its absence is not an argument against. On a third name, I looked for one and I do not find a clear case. Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley were key to individual milestones, but the Statutes limit us to three and the invention line runs through Katori, while the accuracy line runs through Ye. Adding a third from the experimental teams would also require us to say why not the others, and I do not think the evidence supports that choice. I prefer a clean two-name prize and a citation that does not claim more than that.

responses.point: Pearce, who wrote that the committee must be able to state what is new in the lattice clock, also asked whether a two-part prize pairing B005 with a subset of the IceCube names would be acceptable.
responses.response: I can offer one-sentence statement he asked for: it is the invention of trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that many atoms can be interrogated without perturbation, which neither the comb nor the single ion supplied. On the two-part question, I would not support a B005 plus partial B035 configuration. Taking only one of Halzen, Karle and Spiering would be unfair to the omitted names, and for the reasons I gave in round 1 I am not yet sure that the right three are identified at IceCube, since AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND history and the collaboration of several hundred people sit behind them. I would keep B035 for a later year after outside expert views on roles.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether waiting for the SI redefinition would add maturity or only delay, and whether the lattice clock is a discovery in the Nobel sense or precision engineering.
responses.response: I think waiting adds delay, not maturity. The maturity evidence is experimental and is already there: independent reproduction, comparisons between laboratories, and uncertainties that have been checked against each other. A redefinition would confirm the decision of the metrology community but would not add to the physics. On discovery versus engineering, I would say the committee has awarded invention of measurement tools before when they gave access to something previously unobservable. I understand he does not regard that as settled, and I would accept that disagreement; I do not want to treat his KPZ preference as a lesser case, but I still cannot evaluate its experimental verification from the files.

responses.point: Danielsson notes that only tightened bounds on constant variation have been obtained so far, and asks whether a measured effect is needed for the physics to be decisive.
responses.response: I do not think a measured variation is required. The prize would be for the invention and realization of the clock, which has already produced new measurements, such as gravitational redshift over centimetre scales, that were not possible before. The tightened bounds are a use of the tool, not the basis of the award. This is the reason I want the citation to speak about the clock and the new regime of precision, and not about tests of fundamental physics that have not yet found a deviation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, after weighing the 2005 and 2012 prizes, regards the lattice clock as a distinct invention; I think yes, but others hold the view that it is not settled.

Primary-source priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal (2001-2003) and the first strontium lattice-clock measurements, and the early lattice-clock work of other groups, to be checked by outside experts.
Whether Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde or Derevianko has a claim that the two-name configuration would overlook; I have not found a case that justifies a third name.

For my alternatives, B014 needs a decision on the credit for Yuan Cao and other experimental groups and on the pairing mechanism, and B015 needs a resolution of the four-way credit among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger.
I have dropped B051 from my alternatives because it has no support from colleagues and because I would recuse on it; this is a procedural choice and not a verdict on its science.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional connection to Katori or Ye is apparent. My general ties to Japanese microscopy communities and the University of Tokyo are not specific to them. I share a Chalmers affiliation with Johansson. I remain an interested party on B051 (Rose, Urban, Haider) because of my own field, and would recuse on it if it advanced; it is not in my final configuration.
